$comment: The people this deployment recognises, and what each is entitled to do. Names appear throughout the record — who approved a rule, who proposed one, who decided a submission — and until now every one of them was a free string. A free string cannot be checked, so 'Sarah Peterson' and 'sarah peterson' and a typo were three different people, and a name nobody recognises was indistinguishable from one everybody does. Roles are what the policy contract checks against: proposing a rule and enacting one are different entitlements, and the difference is the whole of D27. Reviewed like every other config file (D45) rather than editable at runtime — D14 leaves the prototype unauthenticated, so a runtime user admin would be a control with no gate behind it. THIS IS NOT AUTHENTICATION. It says who is recognised and what they may do; it does not verify that whoever typed a name is that person. Design §19.5.

$roles.compliance-agent: Reviews submissions and records decisions (approve, reject, return). The persona the interface is designed for (§2.1).
$roles.policy-approver: Enacts a rule — the named human approval D27 requires before anything reaches force. The role ui-design §2.3 records as the notable gap.
$roles.policy-author: Puts a rule forward for approval. May draft with a model; is answerable for proposing it. Cannot enact their own proposal.
$roles.administrator: Approves which models may read a label (config/approved-models.json, D29).

$separationOfDuty: A policy-author is deliberately not a policy-approver. Sarah Peterson may propose a rule and may not enact it; the administrator may enact and does not propose. That separation is what makes an approval mean something — a proposal signed off by the person who made it is not a review, and D27 asks for a review. The contract enforces it (see policy.ts).
